# Overview



**gmx_MMPBSA** is an open-source computational chemistry tool that bridges two of the most widely used molecular dynamics ecosystems — **GROMACS** and **AMBER** — to perform end-state free energy calculations. Built as a faithful adaptation of AMBER's `MMPBSA.py`, it allows researchers who simulate their biomolecular systems with GROMACS to leverage the mature implicit solvent models (Generalized Born, Poisson–Boltzmann, 3D-RISM, and others) from AmberTools for binding free energy estimation, decomposition analysis, alanine scanning, and entropy calculations. The project is licensed under GPLv3 and requires Python 3.11 alongside AmberTools ≥ 20.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L15), [setup.py](setup.py#L27-L48), [GMXMMPBSA/__init__.py](GMXMMPBSA/__init__.py#L30-L36)

![gmx_MMPBSA Logo](https://github.com/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/docs/assets/logo.svg?raw=true)

## The Big Picture: How gmx_MMPBSA Works

At its core, gmx_MMPBSA follows a **pipeline architecture** that converts GROMACS-native simulation outputs into AMBER-compatible formats, runs implicit solvent energy calculations on each snapshot, and then aggregates the results into statistical summaries. The entire workflow is orchestrated by the `MMPBSA_App` class in [`main.py`](GMXMMPBSA/main.py), which serves as the central driver for every calculation session.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["GROMACS Input Files<br/>.tpr · .xtc/.trr · .ndx"] --> B["Topology Conversion<br/>CheckMakeTop"]
    B --> C["AMBER Topology Files<br/>.prmtop · .inpcrd"]
    C --> D["Trajectory Processing<br/>make_trajectories"]
    D --> E["Energy Calculations<br/>GB / PB / RISM / GBNSR6"]
    E --> F["Entropy Calculations<br/>nmode / quasi-harmonic / IE / C²"]
    F --> G["Output Generation<br/>FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA.dat"]
    G --> H["GUI Analyzer<br/>gmx_MMPBSA_ana"]
    
    style A fill:#4CAF50,color:#fff
    style C fill:#2196F3,color:#fff
    style H fill:#FF9800,color:#fff
```

The pipeline begins with **topology conversion**, where the `CheckMakeTop` class reads GROMACS `.tpr` and `.top` files, generates PDB coordinates, and uses ParmEd alongside `tleap` to produce AMBER `.prmtop` (topology) and `.inpcrd` (coordinate) files. Next, **trajectory processing** via `make_trajectories` and `cpptraj` strips solvents, applies image centering, and splits the trajectory into per-MPI-rank chunks. The **energy calculation engine** then dispatches snapshots to external programs (sander, mmpbsa_py_energy, gbnsr6) for implicit solvent evaluation. Finally, results are parsed, statistics are computed, and output files are written — with an optional launch of the interactive GUI analyzer.

Sources: [GMXMMPBSA/main.py](GMXMMPBSA/main.py#L109-L180), [GMXMMPBSA/make_top.py](GMXMMPBSA/make_top.py#L76-L123), [GMXMMPBSA/make_trajs.py](GMXMMPBSA/make_trajs.py#L43-L48)

## Project Structure

The codebase is organized into a clear module hierarchy under the `GMXMMPBSA/` package. Each module encapsulates a single responsibility within the calculation pipeline, making the system modular and extensible.

```
gmx_MMPBSA/
├── GMXMMPBSA/                    # Core package
│   ├── main.py                   # MMPBSA_App — central orchestrator (1526 lines)
│   ├── calculation.py            # Calculation class hierarchy (1226 lines)
│   ├── make_top.py               # GROMACS → AMBER topology conversion (1758 lines)
│   ├── make_trajs.py             # Trajectory processing via cpptraj (747 lines)
│   ├── input_parser.py           # Input file definition & parser (664 lines)
│   ├── commandlineparser.py      # CLI argument parsing (313 lines)
│   ├── parm_setup.py             # AMBER topology validation & masking (878 lines)
│   ├── API.py                    # Python API for post-hoc analysis (1051 lines)
│   ├── output_file.py            # Final output generation (631 lines)
│   ├── amber_outputs.py          # AMBER output file parsers
│   ├── createinput.py            # sander/rism input file generation
│   ├── infofile.py               # Calculation metadata persistence
│   ├── app.py                    # CLI entry points
│   ├── fake_mpi.py               # MPI stub for single-process mode
│   ├── exceptions.py             # Custom exception hierarchy
│   ├── utils.py                  # Shared utility functions
│   ├── timer.py                  # Performance timing
│   ├── tester.py                 # Built-in example test runner
│   └── analyzer/                 # Interactive GUI analyzer
│       ├── gui.py                # Main window (PyQt5/PyQt6)
│       ├── plots.py              # Chart & table rendering
│       ├── dialogs.py            # Configuration dialogs
│       ├── parametertree/        # Parameter tree widgets
│       └── style/                # Themes & assets
├── GMXMMPBSA.sh                  # Shell wrapper script
├── setup.py                      # Package installation
├── examples/                     # 20+ worked examples
└── docs/                         # Documentation source (MkDocs)
```

Sources: [GMXMMPBSA/app.py](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L40-L166), [setup.py](setup.py#L30-L58)

## Key Capabilities

gmx_MMPBSA provides a comprehensive suite of molecular mechanics methods for binding free energy estimation. The following table summarizes the core capabilities and the calculation modules that implement them.

| Capability | Description | Key Module |
|---|---|---|
| **GB Calculations** | Generalized Born implicit solvent models (igb 1–8, ALPB) | [`calculation.py`](GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py#L300-L332) |
| **PB Calculations** | Poisson–Boltzmann solvers (linear/nonlinear, membrane support) | [`calculation.py`](GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py#L572-L584) |
| **GBNSR6** | Surface-area generalized Born with optimized radii | [`calculation.py`](GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py#L873-L929) |
| **3D-RISM** | 3D Reference Interaction Site Model solvation | [`calculation.py`](GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py#L367-L478) |
| **Normal Mode Entropy** | Quasi-harmonic vibrational entropy via nmode | [`calculation.py`](GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py#L482-L518) |
| **Quasi-Harmonic Entropy** | Entropy from covariance matrix diagonalization | [`calculation.py`](GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py#L519-L568) |
| **Interaction Entropy** | Entropy from gas-phase energy fluctuations | [`calculation.py`](GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py#L761-L831) |
| **C² Entropy** | Compact entropy estimator from interaction energies | [`calculation.py`](GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py#L833-L871) |
| **Decomposition** | Per-residue energy decomposition (idecomp 1–3) | [`calculation.py`](GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py#L902-L928) |
| **Alanine Scanning** | In-silico mutagenesis to alanine/glycine | [`make_top.py`](GMXMMPBSA/make_top.py#L1017-L1080) |
| **QM/MMGBSA** | Quantum mechanics region in GB calculations | [`input_parser.py`](GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L448-L466) |
| **Stability Analysis** | Fold stability without receptor/ligand separation | [`input_parser.py`](GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L402-L433) |

Sources: [GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py](GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L395-L664), [GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py](GMXMMPBSA/calculation.py#L1-L50)

## Three Ways to Use gmx_MMPBSA

The project exposes three distinct entry points, each registered as a console script in [`setup.py`](setup.py#L53-L56). These cover the full spectrum from one-shot command-line calculations to programmatic integration and interactive visual analysis.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Entry["Entry Points"]
        CLI["gmx_MMPBSA<br/>Command-line calculator"]
        ANA["gmx_MMPBSA_ana<br/>Interactive GUI analyzer"]
        TEST["gmx_MMPBSA_test<br/>Built-in example runner"]
        API2["Python API<br/>MMPBSA_API class"]
    end
    
    subgraph CLI_Flow["CLI Flow"]
        C1["Parse arguments"] --> C2["Build topologies"] --> C3["Process trajectories"]
        C3 --> C4["Run energy calculations"] --> C5["Write output files"]
    end
    
    subgraph ANA_Flow["Analyzer Flow"]
        A1["Load .info files"] --> A2["Select energy/entropy data"] --> A3["Interactive charts & tables"]
    end
    
    subgraph API_Flow["API Flow"]
        P1["Load results"] --> P2["Filter/query data"] --> P3["Custom Python analysis"]
    end
    
    CLI --> CLI_Flow
    ANA --> ANA_Flow
    API2 --> API_Flow
    TEST --> CLI_Flow
    
    style Entry fill:#E8F5E9
    style CLI fill:#4CAF50,color:#fff
    style ANA fill:#FF9800,color:#fff
    style API2 fill:#2196F3,color:#fff
```

**Command-line interface** (`gmx_MMPBSA`) is the primary workflow. Users specify a GROMACS structure file (`.tpr`), trajectory files (`.xtc`/`.trr`), an index file (`.ndx`), and an input configuration file. The `MMPBSA_App` class orchestrates the entire pipeline from topology conversion through final output generation. MPI parallelism is supported natively — the same command works on a laptop or an HPC cluster.

**GUI analyzer** (`gmx_MMPBSA_ana`) is a PyQt5/PyQt6 desktop application that reads the `.info` metadata files produced by calculations. It provides interactive energy bar charts, per-frame line plots, heatmaps, decomposition tables, and multi-system correlation analysis — all without re-running any calculations.

**Python API** (`MMPBSA_API`) enables programmatic access to all calculated energies, entropies, and decomposition data as pandas DataFrames. This is ideal for researchers who want to integrate gmx_MMPBSA results into custom analysis pipelines using numpy, scipy, or machine learning libraries.

Sources: [GMXMMPBSA/app.py](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L40-L145), [GMXMMPBSA/API.py](GMXMMPBSA/API.py#L195-L198), [GMXMMPBSA/analyzer/gui.py](GMXMMPBSA/analyzer/gui.py#L35-L60)

## Supported System Types

One of gmx_MMPBSA's distinguishing strengths is its broad support for different biomolecular system types. The `examples/` directory contains over 20 complete, runnable examples that demonstrate these capabilities. Each example includes input files, reference structures, and ready-to-run configurations.

| System Type | Example Directory | Key Considerations |
|---|---|---|
| Protein–Ligand | `Protein_ligand/` | Single and multiple trajectory protocols |
| Protein–Protein | `Protein_protein/` | Standard MM/PBSA workflow |
| Protein–DNA | `Protein_DNA/` | Nucleic acid parameterization |
| Protein–DNA–RNA–Ion–Ligand | `Protein_DNA_RNA_Ion_ligand/` | Multi-component systems |
| Protein–Glycan | `Protein_glycan/` | GLYCAM force field support |
| Protein–Membrane | `Protein_membrane/` | Implicit membrane PB model |
| Metalloprotein–Ligand | `Metalloprotein_ligand/` | Metal ion parameterization |
| CHARMM Force Field | `Protein_ligand_CHARMMff/` | CHARMM-to-AMBER conversion |
| OPLS Force Field | `OPLS/` | OPLS parameter handling |
| PSF/DCD (NAMD) | `psf_dcd/` | Cross-tool compatibility |
| Alanine Scanning | `Alanine_scanning/` | In-silico mutagenesis |
| Decomposition Analysis | `Decomposition_analysis/` | Per-residue energy breakdown |
| Entropy Calculations | `Entropy_calculations/` | nmode, IE, C², quasi-harmonic |
| COVID-19 Proteins | `COVID-19_related_proteins/` | Real-world application |
| Correlation Studies | `Correlation/` | Multi-system comparison |
| QM/MMGBSA | `QM_MMGBSA/` | Semi-empirical QM region |
| GBNSR6 | `GBNSR6/` | Optimized GB surface model |

Sources: [examples/README.md](examples/README.md), [GMXMMPBSA/data/gmxMMPBSA/](GMXMMPBSA/data/gmxMMPBSA/), [GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py](GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L402-L466)

## Dependencies and Requirements

gmx_MMPBSA requires a specific, well-defined software stack. The dependency chain is managed through both `pip` packages and external system-level tools.

| Requirement | Version | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.11 | Runtime environment (strict pin) |
| AmberTools | ≥ 20 | sander, mmpbsa_py_energy, cpptraj, tleap |
| GROMACS | Any | Simulation engine (provides input files) |
| ParmEd | ≥ 4.2.2 | Topology format conversion |
| mpi4py | 4.0.1 | MPI parallelism support |
| numpy | 1.26.4 | Numerical computation |
| pandas | 1.5.3 | Data handling (API & output) |
| matplotlib | 3.7.3 | Plotting (GUI analyzer) |
| PyQt5/PyQt6 | — | GUI analyzer (optional) |
| tqdm | — | Progress bars |

Sources: [setup.py](setup.py#L41-L48), [GMXMMPBSA/__init__.py](GMXMMPBSA/__init__.py#L33-L34), [GMXMMPBSA/main.py](GMXMMPBSA/main.py#L36-L47)

# Quick Start



This guide walks you through your first binding free energy calculation with **gmx_MMPBSA** — from installation to results — in the shortest path possible. By the end, you will understand the full execution pipeline, the required input files, and how to interpret the output.

## The gmx_MMPBSA Suite at a Glance

gmx_MMPBSA is not a single tool but a suite of three complementary applications, each registered as a console script entry point in [setup.py](setup.py#L52-L56):

| Command | Purpose | Entry Point |
|:--------|:--------|:------------|
| `gmx_MMPBSA` | Core calculation engine — performs MM/PB(GB)SA free energy analyses | `GMXMMPBSA.app:gmxmmpbsa` |
| `gmx_MMPBSA_ana` | Interactive GUI analyzer — visualizes and compares results | `GMXMMPBSA.app:gmxmmpbsa_ana` |
| `gmx_MMPBSA_test` | Validation runner — tests installation with real examples | `GMXMMPBSA.app:gmxmmpbsa_test` |

The relationship between these components follows a linear pipeline: **prepare inputs → run calculation → analyze results**.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Input Files<br/>tpr + ndx + xtc + .in] --> B[gmx_MMPBSA<br/>Calculation Engine]
    B --> C[Output Files<br/>.dat + .csv + _info]
    C --> D[gmx_MMPBSA_ana<br/>GUI Analyzer]
    B -.-> E[gmx_MMPBSA_test<br/>Installation Validator]
```

Sources: [setup.py](setup.py#L52-L56), [app.py](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L41-L167)

## Prerequisites

Before running any calculation, ensure your system meets these requirements:

**Software dependencies:**

| Dependency | Minimum Version | Purpose |
|:-----------|:----------------|:--------|
| Python | 3.11 | Runtime environment (hard requirement) |
| GROMACS | 4.x / 5.x / 20xx.x | Provides topology and trajectory files |
| AmberTools | ≥ 20 | Provides sander/PB solvers and ParmEd |
| MPI library | OpenMPI | Required for parallel calculations |

The Python version constraint is enforced programmatically at install time — the setup script will refuse to install on any Python version other than 3.11 [setup.py](setup.py#L26-L27). The full conda environment specification is available in [env.yml](docs/env.yml#L1-L25).

> [!TIP]
> **Installation shortcut**: Download the [env.yml](docs/env.yml) file and run `conda env create --file env.yml && conda activate gmxMMPBSA` to create a fully configured environment with GROMACS, AmberTools, and all Python dependencies in one step. This is the recommended approach over manual AmberTools compilation.

For detailed installation instructions covering conda, pip, and AmberTools compilation paths, see [Installation](1-overview).

## Understanding the Execution Pipeline

A gmx_MMPBSA calculation proceeds through a well-defined sequence of stages. Understanding this pipeline helps you diagnose issues when things go wrong.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Stage 1: Input
        A[Command-line arguments] --> B[Parse & validate]
        C[mmpbsa.in file] --> B
    end

    subgraph Stage 2: Topology Conversion
        B --> D[Convert GROMACS → AMBER<br/>via ParmEd]
        D --> E[Generate .prmtop files<br/>for complex/receptor/ligand]
    end

    subgraph Stage 3: Trajectory Processing
        E --> F[Extract frames<br/>from .xtc/.trr]
        F --> G[Convert to AMBER<br/>format .mdcrd]
    end

    subgraph Stage 4: Energy Calculation
        G --> H[Run sander per frame<br/>GB/PB/RISM/NMODE]
        H --> I[Collect per-frame<br/>energy data]
    end

    subgraph Stage 5: Output
        I --> J[Parse results<br/>statistics]
        J --> K[Write .dat + .csv<br/>output files]
    end
```

The entry point function in [app.py](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L41-L105) orchestrates this entire flow: it instantiates `MMPBSA_App`, parses arguments, reads the input file, converts topologies via `make_prmtops()`, processes trajectories via `file_setup()`, runs calculations via `run_mmpbsa()`, and writes final outputs. The `main.MMPBSA_App` class ([main.py](GMXMMPBSA/main.py#L64-L65)) is the central driver that holds all state throughout the pipeline.

## Preparing Your Files

gmx_MMPBSA expects a specific set of input files prepared from your GROMACS MD simulation. Here is the complete checklist:

### Required Files

| File | Flag | Format | Description |
|:-----|:-----|:-------|:------------|
| Input parameters | `-i` | `.in` | Calculation configuration (namelist format) |
| Structure file | `-cs` | `.tpr` or `.pdb` | Complex structure with coordinates and topology |
| Index file | `-ci` | `.ndx` | GROMACS index defining receptor/ligand groups |
| Trajectory | `-ct` | `.xtc`, `.trr`, or `.pdb` | Fitted, PBC-removed MD trajectory |

### Required Parameters

| Parameter | Flag | Format | Description |
|:----------|:-----|:-------|:------------|
| Receptor group | `-cg` | integer | Group number for receptor in index file |
| Ligand group | `-cg` | integer | Group number for ligand in index file (second value) |

### Conditionally Required Files

| File | Flag | When Needed |
|:-----|:-----|:------------|
| Topology | `-cp` | When no `.mol2` is provided for the ligand |
| Ligand `.mol2` | `-lm` | Protein–small-molecule complexes without `-cp` |
| Reference structure | `-cr` | When chain ID assignment matters (recommended) |

The command-line argument definitions are centralized in [commandlineparser.py](GMXMMPBSA/commandlineparser.py#L174-L234), where each flag has a type-checking decorator ensuring only valid file extensions are accepted.

### Trajectory Preprocessing

Your trajectory must be **fitted and PBC-removed** before feeding it to gmx_MMPBSA. The standard GROMACS workflow:

```bash
# Create a combined group for centering (assuming receptor=1, ligand=12)
gmx make_ndx -n index.ndx -o new_index.ndx
# > 1 | 12
# > q

# Remove PBC and center
gmx trjconv -s md.tpr -f md.xtc -o md_noPBC.xtc -pbc mol -center -n new_index.ndx -ur compact
# center: 20  (the combined group)
# output: 0

# Fit to reference (optional but recommended)
gmx trjconv -s md.tpr -f md_noPBC.xtc -o md_fit.xtc -n new_index.ndx -fit rot+trans
# fit: 20
# output: 0
```

## Creating the Input File

The input file uses Amber's **namelist format** — Fortran-style `&namelist /` blocks containing key-value pairs. The full schema is defined in [input_parser.py](GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L396-L664) with eight namelists: `general`, `gb`, `pb`, `gbnsr6`, `rism`, `ala`, `decomp`, and `nmode`.

### Minimal Input File for GB Calculation

Create a file named `mmpbsa.in`:

```fortran
&general
sys_name="Prot-Lig",
startframe=1,
endframe=10,
/
&gb
igb=5, saltcon=0.150,
/
```

This is the exact format used in the shipped examples ([Protein_ligand/ST/mmpbsa.in](examples/Protein_ligand/ST/mmpbsa.in#L1-L14)).

### Input File Parameters Explained

| Namelist | Key Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|:---------|:-------------|:--------|:--------|
| `&general` | `startframe` | 1 | First frame to analyze |
| `&general` | `endframe` | 9999999 | Last frame to analyze |
| `&general` | `interval` | 1 | Frame sampling stride |
| `&general` | `forcefields` | `oldff/leaprc.ff99SB, leaprc.gaff` | AMBER force fields for topology conversion |
| `&gb` | `igb` | 5 | GB model (1=GB1, 2=OBC1, 5=OBC2, 7=OBC2 w/ NL, 8=GBNeck) |
| `&gb` | `saltcon` | 0.0 | Salt concentration in M |
| `&pb` | `ipb` | 2 | PB solver (1=Linear, 2=Linear w/ optimize) |

> [!TIP]
> **Quick template generation**: Instead of writing input files manually, use `gmx_MMPBSA --create_input gb` to auto-generate a complete template file named `mmpbsa.in` with all available options documented inline. Other valid choices are `pb`, `rism`, `ala`, `decomp`, `nmode`, and `all`.

For the complete parameter reference including PB, RISM, decomposition, and entropy options, proceed to [Input File Reference](3-input-file-reference).

## Running Your First Calculation

### Serial Execution

Navigate to the directory containing all your input files and run:

```bash
gmx_MMPBSA -O -i mmpbsa.in -cs com.tpr -ct com_traj.xtc \
  -ci index.ndx -cg 3 4 -cp topol.top \
  -o FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA.dat -eo FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA.csv
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|:-----|:--------|
| `-O` | Overwrite existing output files |
| `-i` | Input parameters file |
| `-cs` | Complex structure (.tpr) |
| `-ct` | Complex trajectory (.xtc) |
| `-ci` | Index file (.ndx) |
| `-cg 3 4` | Receptor=group 3, Ligand=group 4 |
| `-cp` | Complex topology (.top) |
| `-o` | Final statistics output (.dat) |
| `-eo` | Per-frame CSV output (all energies) |

### Parallel Execution (Recommended)

MPI parallelism distributes frames across processors, dramatically reducing wall-clock time:

```bash
mpirun -np 4 gmx_MMPBSA -O -i mmpbsa.in -cs com.tpr -ct com_traj.xtc \
  -ci index.ndx -cg 3 4 -cp topol.top \
  -o FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA.dat -eo FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA.csv
```

**Important caveats about MPI execution:**

- MPI is used **only for the energy calculation stage** (sander invocations). Topology conversion, trajectory splitting, and output parsing all run on a single thread regardless of processor count.
- You do **not** need GROMACS compiled with MPI — `gmx` (non-MPI) works correctly since only `sander` from AmberTools is parallelized via `mpirun`.
- Parallel scaling degrades when the number of threads approaches the frame count, and 3D-RISM calculations may actually run **slower** in parallel because they lose the convergence benefit of using previous solutions as initial guesses.

Sources: [gmx_MMPBSA_running.md](docs/gmx_MMPBSA_running.md#L100-L167)

### Stability Mode

For protein stability calculations (no binding partner), add the `-s` flag and provide only complex parameters:

```bash
gmx_MMPBSA -O -i mmpbsa.in -s -cs com.tpr -ct com_traj.xtc \
  -ci index.ndx -cg 3 4 -cp topol.top -o FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA.dat
```

The `-s` / `--stability` flag ([commandlineparser.py](GMXMMPBSA/commandlineparser.py#L168-L172)) tells gmx_MMPBSA to skip the receptor/ligand separation and treat the entire complex as a single entity.

## Verifying with Built-in Examples

gmx_MMPBSA ships with over 20 complete example systems in the [`examples/`](examples/) directory. The `gmx_MMPBSA_test` command automates running these to verify your installation:

```bash
# Run fast tests (default) — 9 quick systems
gmx_MMPBSA_test

# Run a specific example (e.g., Protein-Ligand single trajectory)
gmx_MMPBSA_test -t 3

# Run minimal set to validate installation
gmx_MMPBSA_test -t 1

# Run all examples (takes a long time)
gmx_MMPBSA_test -t 0
```

Test identifiers are defined in [commandlineparser.py](GMXMMPBSA/commandlineparser.py#L269-L303). The most useful IDs for beginners:

| ID | System | Speed |
|:---|:-------|:------|
| 2 | Fast test set (default, 9 systems) | Fast |
| 3 | Protein–Ligand (single trajectory) | Fast |
| 4 | Protein–Protein | Fast |
| 5 | Protein–DNA | Fast |
| 6 | Protein–Membrane | Slow |
| 14 | Decomposition Analysis | Fast |
| 17 | Normal Mode Entropy | Slow |

## Understanding the Output

After a successful calculation, gmx_MMPBSA produces several output files:

### Primary Output Files

| File | Default Name | Content |
|:-----|:-------------|:--------|
| Statistics summary | `FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA.dat` | Mean, standard deviation, and error for every energy term |
| Per-frame energies | `FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA.csv` | Every energy component for every frame (only if `-eo` specified) |
| Calculation info | `* _info` | Machine-readable pickle of the full calculation state |

### Key Energy Terms in the Statistics Output

The output `.dat` file contains the standard MM/PB(GB)SA thermodynamic decomposition. The binding free energy is computed as:

```
ΔG_bind = ΔE_MM + ΔG_solv - TΔS
        = (ΔE_vdw + ΔE_ele) + (ΔG_GB/PB + ΔG_SA) - TΔS
```

Each term is reported with mean, standard deviation, and standard error of the mean across all analyzed frames. The `write_final_outputs` method in [main.py](GMXMMPBSA/main.py#L735-L760) handles generation of these statistics.

### Launching the Analyzer

Unless you used the `-nogui` flag, the interactive analyzer (`gmx_MMPBSA_ana`) launches automatically upon calculation completion. You can also launch it manually:

```bash
# Analyze a specific info file
gmx_MMPBSA_ana -f FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA_info

# Analyze all info files in current directory recursively
gmx_MMPBSA_ana -f . -r
```

The analyzer requires PyQt5 or PyQt6 and provides interactive charts, energy term comparisons, and publication-quality figure export. For a full walkthrough, see [Interactive Visualization](16-interactive-visualization).

## Quick Reference: Common Command Patterns

| Scenario | Command |
|:---------|:--------|
| Generate input template | `gmx_MMPBSA --create_input gb` |
| List all input options | `gmx_MMPBSA --input-file-help` |
| Run GB calculation (serial) | `gmx_MMPBSA -O -i mmpbsa.in -cs com.tpr -ct traj.xtc -ci index.ndx -cg 1 13` |
| Run with topology file | `gmx_MMPBSA -O -i mmpbsa.in -cs com.tpr -ct traj.xtc -ci index.ndx -cg 1 13 -cp topol.top` |
| Run with MPI | `mpirun -np 4 gmx_MMPBSA -O -i mmpbsa.in -cs com.tpr -ct traj.xtc -ci index.ndx -cg 1 13` |
| Stability calculation | `gmx_MMPBSA -O -s -i mmpbsa.in -cs com.tpr -ct traj.xtc -ci index.ndx -cg 1 13` |
| Clean temporary files | `gmx_MMPBSA --clean` |
| Re-parse existing output | `gmx_MMPBSA --rewrite-output` |
| Test installation | `gmx_MMPBSA_test -t 2` |
| Enable shell autocompletion | `source /path/to/GMXMMPBSA/GMXMMPBSA.sh` |

The autocompletion script [GMXMMPBSA.sh](GMXMMPBSA/GMXMMPBSA.sh#L1-L112) provides tab-completion for all flags and file extensions in bash — a small productivity boost that prevents typos in long command lines.

- **[Output Files Guide](4-output-files-guide)** — Detailed breakdown of every output file format, CSV column meanings, and statistics interpretation

# Input File Reference



The input file is the single point of configuration that drives every gmx_MMPBSA calculation. It tells the program which solvation models to run, how to handle your GROMACS topology, which frames to process, and what optional analyses to perform. This page covers the file's architecture, every namelist and its variables, and the conventions you need to follow when writing or modifying one.

## Architecture of the Input File

At the parsing level, the input file is an ordered collection of **namelists**—Fortran-derived blocks introduced by `&name` and terminated by `/`. Each namelist groups logically related variables, and the parser (`InputFile` class in [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L171-L394)) matches blocks by comparing the user-provided name against the first *N* characters of the registered full name. The `&general` namelist is always present; the remaining namelists are each guarded by a **trigger variable** (e.g., `gbrun`, `pbrun`, `decomprun`) that the parser flips to `True` when it encounters that block, signalling downstream code to activate the corresponding calculation [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L230-L253).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["mmpbsa.in"] --> B["InputFile.Parse()"]
    B --> C{"&general block?"}
    C -- Yes --> D["Always parsed<br/>No trigger"]
    C -- No --> E{"Other block?"}
    E -- "&gb" --> F["Set gbrun = True"]
    E -- "&pb" --> G["Set pbrun = True"]
    E -- "&gbnsr6" --> H["Set gbnsr6run = True"]
    E -- "&rism" --> I["Set rismrun = True"]
    E -- "&decomp" --> J["Set decomprun = True"]
    E -- "&alanine_scanning" --> K["Set alarun = True"]
    E -- "&nmode" --> L["Set nmoderun = True"]
    F --> M["create_inputs()<br/>generates .mdin files"]
    G --> M
    H --> M
    I --> M
    J --> M
    K --> M
    L --> M
```

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L171-L253), [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L395-L663)

## File Format and Conventions

gmx_MMPBSA accepts two stylistic variants that are semantically identical. The **new format** places one `variable = value` pair per line with inline comments, resembling GROMACS `*.mdp` files. The **old (classic Amber) format** places multiple comma-separated assignments on the same line. You can even mix both styles within a single file. Strings must be enclosed in single or double quotes; integers and floats are typed as-is; list values are comma- or semicolon-delimited [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L55-L105).

=== "New format (recommended)"

```title="mmpbsa.in"
&general
  sys_name             = "MySystem"
  startframe           = 1
  endframe             = 100
  interval             = 1
  forcefields          = "leaprc.protein.ff14SB"
/

&gb
  igb                  = 5
  saltcon              = 0.150
/
```

=== "Classic Amber format"

```title="mmpbsa.in"
&general
  sys_name = "MySystem", startframe = 1, endframe = 100,
  interval = 1, forcefields = "leaprc.protein.ff14SB"
/

&gb
  igb = 5, saltcon = 0.150
/
```

> [!TIP]
> Every namelist except `&general` is **optional**. Only include the namelists for the calculations you actually want to perform. Including `&gb` automatically activates the GB calculation; including `&pb` activates PB, and so on.

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L55-L105)

## Generating Input Files from the Command Line

You don't have to write an input file from scratch. The `--create_input` flag generates a template pre-populated with sensible defaults for any combination of calculations. This is the recommended starting point for beginners [docs/input_file.md](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/docs/input_file.md#L29-L62).

```bash
# Generate a GB-only template
gmx_MMPBSA -i mmpbsa.in --create_input gb

# Generate a template with GB, PB, and decomposition
gmx_MMPBSA -i mmpbsa.in --create_input gb pb decomp

# Generate all possible sections
gmx_MMPBSA -i mmpbsa.in --create_input all
```

The generated file includes every variable with its default value and a descriptive comment. Review it carefully—some parameters such as `forcefields`, `PBRadii`, and `startframe`/`endframe` must be adjusted for your specific system before running.

## Namelist Overview

The following table summarises every namelist, its trigger, and its purpose. Multiple namelists can coexist in the same input file, enabling combined analyses such as GB + alanine scanning, PB + decomposition, or GB + entropy methods.

| Namelist | Short Form | Trigger Variable | Purpose |
|----------|-----------|-------------------|---------|
| `&general` | `general` | *(always active)* | System-wide settings, topology conversion, entropy flags |
| `&gb` | `gb` | `gbrun` | Generalized Born solvation (also contains QM/MM options) |
| `&gbnsr6` | `gbnsr6` | `gbnsr6run` | GBNSR6 surface-area-free solvation model |
| `&pb` | `pb` | `pbrun` | Poisson-Boltzmann solvation (linear, non-linear, membrane) |
| `&rism` | `rism` | `rismrun` | 3D-RISM integral equation solvation |
| `&alanine_scanning` | `ala` | `alarun` | In-silico alanine/glycine scanning mutagenesis |
| `&decomp` | `decomp` | `decomprun` | Per-residue energy decomposition analysis |
| `&nmode` | `nmode` | `nmoderun` | Normal-mode vibrational entropy approximation |

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L402-L663)

---

## `&general` Namelist

This namelist controls everything that is **not specific to a single solvation model**—frame selection, AMBER topology construction from GROMACS files, entropy methods, and miscellaneous runtime behaviour. It is always parsed regardless of which other namelists are present [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L402-L433).

### Basic Options

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `sys_name` | `str` | `""` | A short label for your system. Appears in output file headers and plots. |
| `startframe` | `int` | `1` | First trajectory frame to analyse (1-based). |
| `endframe` | `int` | `9999999` | Last trajectory frame to analyse. Set lower than the total frames for faster testing. |
| `interval` | `int` | `1` | Stride between analysed frames. `interval = 2` skips every other frame. |

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L405-L408)

### Parameter Options

These variables govern how gmx_MMPBSA converts your GROMACS topology into an AMBER-compatible one via ParmEd. Choosing the correct `forcefields` entry is critical—if it doesn't match the force field used in your GROMACS simulation, the resulting energies will be meaningless [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L410-L416).

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `forcefields` | `list` | `"oldff/leaprc.ff99SB, leaprc.gaff"` | Comma-separated Amber leaprc files used to build the topology. Must match your GROMACS force field. Common values: `leaprc.protein.ff14SB`, `leaprc.protein.ff19SB`, `leaprc.gaff`, `leaprc.lipid17`. |
| `ions_parameters` | `int` | `1` | Selects the ion parameter set (1 = default Jensen/Joung ions). |
| `PBRadii` | `int` | `3` | Selects the Bondi/mbondi radii set for PB and GB calculations. Values: 1–6. |
| `temperature` | `float` | `298.15` | System temperature in Kelvin. Used for entropy calculations and thermochemical corrections. |

> [!TIP]
> The `forcefields` parameter is the single most important setting in the `&general` namelist. For CHARMM-based simulations, use `leaprc.protein.ff14SB` with additional CHARMM-specific leaprc files. See the [Protein_ligand_CHARMMff](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/tree/master/examples/Protein_ligand_CHARMMff) example for the exact configuration.

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L410-L416)

### Entropy Options

gmx_MMPBSA supports four entropy approximations, toggled by flags in the `&general` namelist. These flags instruct the program to perform additional calculations beyond the standard MM/PBSA or MM/GBSA energies [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L418-L421).

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `qh_entropy` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to perform quasi-harmonic entropy calculation via cpptraj. |
| `interaction_entropy` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to compute Interaction Entropy (IE) from trajectory fluctuations. |
| `ie_segment` | `int` | `25` | Number of frames per segment for the IE moving-average window. |
| `c2_entropy` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to compute the C2 entropy correction. |

Note that `qh_entropy` and `c2_entropy` are independent of the `&nmode` namelist, while normal-mode entropy requires the separate `&nmode` block. You can combine interaction entropy with any solvation model (GB, PB, GBNSR6, or RISM) by simply setting `interaction_entropy = 1` alongside the corresponding solvation namelist.

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L418-L421)

### Miscellaneous Options

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `assign_chainID` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to assign chain identifiers from the structure. Useful for CHARMM systems or when chain info was lost during GROMACS preprocessing. |
| `exp_ki` | `list` | `[0.0]` | Experimental inhibition constant(s) in nM. Used to correlate computed ΔG with experimental data. |
| `full_traj` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to print the full concatenated trajectory plus per-thread trajectories. |
| `gmx_path` | `str` | `""` | Explicit path to the GROMACS executable. Leave empty for auto-detection. |
| `keep_files` | `int` | `2` | Controls post-calculation file retention. `0` = delete all, `1` = keep essential files, `2` = keep everything. |
| `netcdf` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to use NetCDF format for intermediate trajectory files (smaller, faster I/O). |
| `solvated_trajectory` | `int` | `1` | Set to `1` if the input trajectory contains solvent (the default). Set to `0` if the trajectory is already stripped of water and ions. |
| `verbose` | `int` | `1` | Controls output verbosity. `0` = minimal, `1` = standard (all energy terms), `2` = detailed. |

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L424-L433)

---

## `&gb` Namelist

The Generalized Born namelist configures the GB implicit-solvent model used by the AMBER sander engine. It also contains QM/MMGBSA options when `ifqnt = 1` is set. Including this namelist activates the GB calculation (trigger: `gbrun`) [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L435-L470).

### Basic GB Options

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `igb` | `int` | `5` | GB model selection. Common values: `1` (GB1), `2` (GB2/OBC1), `5` (GB5/OBC2), `7` (GB7), `8` (GB8). Model 5 is the most widely used default. |
| `intdiel` | `float` | `1.0` | Internal (solute) dielectric constant. Higher values reduce electrostatic interactions. |
| `extdiel` | `float` | `78.5` | External (solvent) dielectric constant. 78.5 approximates water at 25 °C. |
| `saltcon` | `float` | `0.0` | Salt concentration in mol/L. Use `0.150` for physiological conditions. |
| `surften` | `float` | `0.0072` | Surface tension (kcal/mol/Å²) for the nonpolar solvation term (LCPO method). |
| `surfoff` | `float` | `0.0` | Surface tension offset (kcal/mol) added to the nonpolar term. |
| `molsurf` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to use the Connolly molecular surface (`molsurf`) instead of LCPO for the nonpolar term. |
| `msoffset` | `float` | `0.0` | Offset for the molsurf nonpolar calculation. |
| `probe` | `float` | `1.4` | Solvent probe radius in Å for surface area computation. |
| `alpb` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to use the Analytical Linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (ALPB) model instead of standard GB. |
| `arad_method` | `int` | `1` | Method to estimate effective electrostatic size when `alpb = 1`. |

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L437-L470)

### QM/MMGBSA Options

These variables activate quantum mechanical treatment of selected residues within the GB framework [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L448-L466).

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `ifqnt` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to enable QM/MM calculation. |
| `qm_theory` | `str` | `""` | Semi-empirical QM method: `PM3`, `PM6`, `PM6-PDDG`, `DFTB`, `AM1`, etc. |
| `qm_residues` | `str` | `""` | Residue selection for the QM region. Supports Amber mask syntax or distance-based selection (recommended: `"within 4"`). Must include at least one residue from both receptor and ligand. |
| `com_qmmask` | `str` | `""` | Explicit Amber mask for QM atoms in the complex. Alternative to `qm_residues`. |
| `rec_qmmask` | `str` | `""` | Explicit Amber mask for QM atoms in the receptor. |
| `lig_qmmask` | `str` | `""` | Explicit Amber mask for QM atoms in the ligand. |
| `qmcut` | `float` | `9999` | Cutoff (Å) for QM region interactions. |
| `scfconv` | `float` | `1.0e-8` | SCF convergence criterion in kcal/mol. |
| `peptide_corr` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to apply MM correction to peptide linkages in the QM region. |
| `writepdb` | `int` | `1` | Write a PDB file showing the selected QM region. |

> [!TIP]
> When using QM/MMGBSA, the `qm_residues = "within 4"` distance-based selection is strongly recommended over explicit residue lists. It automatically adapts as your structure changes across trajectory frames. See the [QM_MMGBSA example](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/tree/master/examples/QM_MMGBSA) for a complete working configuration.

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L448-L466)

---

## `&gbnsr6` Namelist

The GBNSR6 namelist configures the **GBNSR6** solvation model, a surface-area-free approach that uses the R6 integral to compute nonpolar solvation without an explicit surface term. It was introduced in sander and provides an alternative to the standard GB+SA combination. Including this block activates the GBNSR6 calculation (trigger: `gbnsr6run`) [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L473-L497).

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `b` | `float` | `0.028` | Uniform offset to the inverse effective radii. |
| `alpb` | `int` | `1` | ALPB correction toggle (enabled by default in GBNSR6). |
| `epsin` | `float` | `1.0` | Solute (internal) dielectric constant. |
| `epsout` | `float` | `78.5` | Solvent (external) dielectric constant. |
| `istrng` | `float` | `0.0` | Ionic strength in mol/L. |
| `rs` | `float` | `0.52` | Dielectric boundary shift relative to the molecular surface (for CHAGB). |
| `dprob` | `float` | `1.4` | Solvent probe radius in Å. |
| `space` | `float` | `0.5` | Grid spacing (Å) for solute molecular surface resolution. |
| `arcres` | `float` | `0.2` | Arc resolution for numerical surface integration. |
| `radiopt` | `int` | `0` | Intrinsic atomic radii set selection (for CHAGB option). |
| `chagb` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to use the CHAGB variant. |
| `roh` | `int` | `1` | RzOH parameter for the CHAGB model (maps to predefined values). |
| `tau` | `float` | `1.47` | τ parameter for the CHAGB model. |
| `cavity_surften` | `float` | `0.005` | Surface tension for the cavity/nonpolar term in GBNSR6. |

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L473-L497)

---

## `&pb` Namelist

The Poisson-Boltzmann namelist is the most parameter-rich block, governing the numerical finite-difference solver for implicit solvation. It supports linear and non-linear PB, implicit membrane environments, and multiple solver options. Including this block activates the PB calculation (trigger: `pbrun`) [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L498-L569).

### Basic PB Options

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `ipb` | `int` | `2` | PB dielectric model. `1` = constant dielectric, `2` = two-concentration model. |
| `inp` | `int` | `1` | Nonpolar solvation method. `1` = standard (cavity+dispersion), `2` = only cavity from SASA. |
| `sander_apbs` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to use APBS as the external PB solver instead of the built-in solver. |
| `indi` | `float` | `1.0` | Internal dielectric constant. |
| `exdi` | `float` | `80.0` | External dielectric constant. |
| `istrng` | `float` | `0.0` | Ionic strength in mol/L. |
| `radiopt` | `int` | `1` | Radii set: `0` = Bondi, `1` = mbondi (recommended), `2` = mbondi2, `3` = mbondi3. |
| `prbrad` | `float` | `1.4` | Probe radius in Å for the PB calculation. |
| `npbopt` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` for non-linear PB (NLPB). `0` = linear PB. |
| `solvopt` | `int` | `1` | Iterative solver. `1` = CG, `2` = relaxed GS, `3` = Sharper GS. |
| `accept` | `float` | `0.001` | Convergence criterion (relative to initial residual). |
| `linit` | `int` | `1000` | Maximum number of SCF iterations. |
| `fillratio` | `float` | `4.0` | Ratio of longest grid dimension to solute dimension. |
| `scale` | `float` | `2.0` | Grid spacing = 1/scale Å. Higher scale = finer grid. |
| `nfocus` | `int` | `2` | Number of electrostatic focusing calculations. |
| `nbuffer` | `float` | `0.0` | Buffer distance (grid units) from solute to grid boundary. |

### Implicit Membrane Options

gmx_MMPBSA supports membrane-embedded proteins through the PB implicit membrane model, where a low-dielectric slab represents the lipid bilayer [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L520-L525).

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `memopt` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to enable the implicit membrane model. |
| `emem` | `float` | `4.0` | Membrane dielectric constant (typically 2–8). |
| `mthick` | `float` | `40.0` | Membrane thickness in Å. |
| `mctrdz` | `float` | `0.0` | Z-axis offset of the membrane centre from the solute centre. |
| `mprob` | `float` | `2.70` | Membrane probe radius in Å. |
| `poretype` | `int` | `1` | Set to `1` to use an exclusion region for channel/pore proteins. |

### Nonpolar and Output Options

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `cavity_surften` | `float` | `0.0378` | Surface tension (kcal/mol/Å²) for the nonpolar cavity term. |
| `cavity_offset` | `float` | `-0.5692` | Offset (kcal/mol) for the nonpolar term. |
| `decompopt` | `int` | `2` | Decomposition scheme when `inp = 2`. |
| `npbverb` | `int` | `0` | Verbose PB output. `1` prints additional solver diagnostics. |

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L498-L569)

---

## `&rism` Namelist

The 3D-RISM namelist configures the integral-equation theory of solvation, which provides both polar and nonpolar solvation free energies from the 3D site distribution functions of solvent molecules. Including this block activates the RISM calculation (trigger: `rismrun`) [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L572-L628).

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `closure` | `list` | `["kh"]` | Closure approximation. `kh` = KH, `kh3` = KH with modified closure, etc. |
| `gfcorrection` | `int` | `0` | Gaussian fluctuation excess chemical potential. |
| `pcpluscorrection` | `int` | `0` | PC+ 3D-RISM correction. |
| `noasympcorr` | `int` | `1` | Toggle for long-range asymptotic corrections. |
| `buffer` | `float` | `14` | Distance (Å) between solute and grid edge. |
| `grdspc` | `list` | `[0.5, 0.5, 0.5]` | Grid spacing in x, y, z (Å). |
| `tolerance` | `list` | `[1.0e-5]` | Convergence tolerance for the iterative solver. |
| `maxstep` | `int` | `10000` | Maximum number of iterative steps. |
| `mdiis_del` | `float` | `0.7` | MDIIS step size. |
| `mdiis_nvec` | `int` | `5` | Number of MDIIS history vectors. |
| `polardecomp` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to decompose solvation energy into polar and nonpolar terms. |
| `rism_verbose` | `int` | `0` | RISM output verbosity level. |

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L572-L628)

---

## `&alanine_scanning` Namelist

This namelist enables in-silico alanine (or glycine) scanning mutagenesis, where each specified residue is sequentially mutated and the binding energy difference is computed. The calculation runs on top of a GB or PB calculation—both namelists must be present. Including this block activates alanine scanning (trigger: `alarun`) [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L630-L640).

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `mutant_res` | `str` | `""` | Residue(s) to mutate. Format: `"ChainID:ResNum"` (e.g., `"R:23"`, `"A:45,A:78"`). |
| `mutant` | `str` | `"ALA"` | Mutation type: `"ALA"` for alanine scanning, `"GLY"` for glycine scanning. |
| `mutant_only` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to compute only the mutant energies (skip wild-type). |
| `cas_intdiel` | `int` | `0` | Set to `1` to automatically adjust `intdiel` based on the amino acid being mutated. |
| `intdiel_nonpolar` | `int` | `1` | Internal dielectric for nonpolar residue mutations (when `cas_intdiel = 1`). |
| `intdiel_polar` | `int` | `3` | Internal dielectric for polar residue mutations. |
| `intdiel_positive` | `int` | `5` | Internal dielectric for positively charged residue mutations. |
| `intdiel_negative` | `int` | `5` | Internal dielectric for negatively charged residue mutations. |

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L630-L640)

---

## `&decomp` Namelist

The decomposition namelist enables per-residue energy decomposition, breaking down the total binding energy into contributions from individual residues. It requires either `&gb` or `&pb` to also be present. Including this block activates decomposition (trigger: `decomprun`) [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L642-L648).

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `idecomp` | `int` | `0` | Decomposition scheme: `1` = 1-body (no pairwise), `2` = 2-body pairwise (gas phase), `3` = 2-body with GB/PB, `4` = 2-body with sidechain decomposition. |
| `dec_verbose` | `int` | `0` | Controls how many energy terms are printed per residue in the decomposition output. |
| `print_res` | `str` | `"within 6"` | Residue selection for detailed output. Supports Amber mask syntax. `"within 6"` selects all residues within 6 Å of the binding interface (recommended). |
| `csv_format` | `int` | `1` | Set to `1` to write decomposition data in CSV format for easy downstream analysis. |

> [!TIP]
> When using `print_res`, always ensure at least one residue from **both** the receptor and the ligand is included. The `"within N"` syntax automatically satisfies this requirement. Explicit residue lists like `"A:45,B:12"` require manual verification.

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L642-L648)

---

## `&nmode` Namelist

The normal-mode namelist configures the vibrational entropy calculation using the AMBER nmode program. It performs a minimisation followed by Hessian diagonalisation for selected frames. Including this block activates the nmode calculation (trigger: `nmoderun`) [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L650-L663).

| Variable | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `nmstartframe` | `int` | `1` | First frame for normal-mode analysis (1-based, relative to the general frame selection). |
| `nmendframe` | `int` | `1000000` | Last frame for normal-mode analysis. |
| `nminterval` | `int` | `1` | Stride between frames selected for nmode. Allows subsampling from the general frame range. |
| `nmode_igb` | `int` | `1` | GB model for the nmode minimisation step. Must be compatible with `igb` in `&gb`. |
| `nmode_istrng` | `float` | `0.0` | Ionic strength for the GB model in nmode (mol/L). |
| `dielc` | `float` | `1.0` | Dielectric constant for the nmode calculation. |
| `drms` | `float` | `0.001` | RMS gradient convergence criterion for minimisation (kcal/mol/Å). |
| `maxcyc` | `int` | `10000` | Maximum number of minimisation cycles. For production runs, `50000` is typical. |

Note that nmode is extremely computationally expensive—each frame requires a full minimisation and Hessian calculation. For testing, reduce `maxcyc` and increase `nminterval` to process fewer frames.

Sources: [input_parser.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L650-L663)

---

## Sample Input Files

The following examples are taken directly from the repository's example directory and illustrate real, working configurations for each calculation type. They are designed for quick testing with the bundled trajectory files—note that some parameters (e.g., `maxcyc`, `endframe`) are deliberately relaxed for speed.

### Basic GB Calculation

This is the simplest possible MM/GBSA setup for a protein-protein system [mmpbsa.in](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/examples/Protein_protein/mmpbsa.in).

```title="examples/Protein_protein/mmpbsa.in"
&general
sys_name="Prot-Prot",
startframe=1,
endframe=10,
forcefields="leaprc.protein.ff14SB",
/
&gb
igb=2, saltcon=0.150,
/
```

### GBNSR6 Calculation

Replaces the standard GB model with GBNSR6—no surface area term needed [mmpbsa.in](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/examples/GBNSR6/mmpbsa.in).

```title="examples/GBNSR6/mmpbsa.in"
&general
sys_name="GBNSR6",
startframe=1,
endframe=10,
forcefields="leaprc.protein.ff14SB"
/
&gbnsr6
istrng=0.15
/
```

### QM/MMGBSA Calculation

Treats residues within 4 Å of the binding interface quantum mechanically using the PM3 method [mmpbsa.in](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/examples/QM_MMGBSA/mmpbsa.in).

```title="examples/QM/MMGBSA/mmpbsa.in"
&general
sys_name="QM/MMGBSA",
startframe=5,
endframe=14,
PBRadii=2,
forcefields="oldff/leaprc.ff99SB,leaprc.gaff"
/
&gb
igb=1, saltcon=0.150,
ifqnt=1, qm_theory=PM3,
qm_residues="within 4"
/
```

### PB with Implicit Membrane

Configures the Poisson-Boltzmann solver with an implicit lipid bilayer for membrane-embedded proteins [mmpbsa.in](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/examples/Protein_membrane/mmpbsa.in).

```title="examples/Protein_membrane/mmpbsa.in"
&general
sys_name="Prot-Memb",
startframe=1,
endframe=4,
/
&pb
memopt=1, emem=7.0, indi=4.0,
mctrdz=-10.383, mthick=36.086, poretype=1,
radiopt=0, istrng=0.150, fillratio=1.25, inp=2,
sasopt=0, solvopt=2, ipb=1, bcopt=10, nfocus=1,
linit=1000, eneopt=1, cutfd=7.0, cutnb=99.0,
maxarcdot=15000, npbverb=1,
/
```

### Alanine Scanning

Combines a GB calculation with per-residue alanine scanning for residue R:23 [mmpbsa.in](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/examples/Alanine_scanning/mmpbsa.in).

```title="examples/Alanine_scanning/mmpbsa.in"
&general
sys_name="Alanine_Scanning",
startframe=1,
endframe=10,
forcefields="leaprc.protein.ff14SB",
PBRadii=4,
/
&gb
igb=8, saltcon=0.150,
/
&alanine_scanning
mutant='ALA', mutant_res='R:23', cas_intdiel=1
/
```

### Decomposition Analysis

Per-residue decomposition using the pairwise scheme with GB [mmpbsa.in](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/examples/Decomposition_analysis/mmpbsa.in).

```title="examples/Decomposition_analysis/mmpbsa.in"
&general
sys_name="Decomposition",
startframe=1,
endframe=10,
forcefields="leaprc.protein.ff14SB"
/
&gb
igb=5, saltcon=0.150,
/
&decomp
idecomp=2, dec_verbose=3,
print_res="within 4"
/
```

### Interaction Entropy

Combines a GB calculation with the Interaction Entropy approximation [mmpbsa.in](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/examples/Entropy_calculations/Interaction_Entropy/mmpbsa.in).

```title="examples/Entropy_calculations/Interaction_Entropy/mmpbsa.in"
&general
sys_name="IE",
startframe=1,
endframe=10,
interaction_entropy=1, ie_segment=50, temperature=303.15
/
&gb
igb=2, saltcon=0.150,
/
```

### Normal-Mode Entropy

Full MM/GBSA + nmode entropy pipeline [mmpbsa.in](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/examples/Entropy_calculations/nmode/mmpbsa.in).

```title="examples/Entropy_calculations/nmode/mmpbsa.in"
&general
sys_name="NMode",
startframe=1,
endframe=10,
forcefields="leaprc.protein.ff14SB",
PBRadii=2,
/
&gb
igb=1, saltcon=0.150,
/
&nmode
nmstartframe=3,
nmendframe=10,
nminterval=1,
maxcyc=5, drms=2,
/
```

## Validation and Parsing Pipeline

Understanding how your input file is consumed helps you debug issues faster. The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow from file on disk to the `.mdin` files consumed by sander:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["mmpbsa.in<br/>(user-written)"] --> B["InputFile.Parse()"]
    B --> C["INPUT dict<br/>(nested namelists)"]
    C --> D{"&gb present?"}
    D -- Yes --> E["SanderGBInput<br/>.mdin generator"]
    C --> F{"&pb present?"}
    F -- Yes --> G["SanderPBSAInput<br/>.mdin generator"]
    C --> H{"&gbnsr6 present?"}
    H -- Yes --> I["GBNSR6Input<br/>.mdin generator"]
    C --> J{"&decomp present?"}
    J -- Yes --> K["SanderGBDecomp /<br/>SanderPBDecomp"]
    E --> L["*.mdin files<br/>(sander input)"]
    G --> L
    I --> L
    K --> L
    L --> M["sander /<br/>sander.APBS"]
```

The `create_inputs()` function in [createinput.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/createinput.py#L49-L310) orchestrates this process. It inspects the parsed `INPUT` dictionary, checks which triggers are active, and instantiates the appropriate sander input writer class. Each writer class (e.g., `SanderGBInput`, `SanderPBSAInput`) constructs the Amber-format `.mdin` file that sander reads at runtime.

Sources: [createinput.py](/Valdes-Tresanco-MS/gmx_MMPBSA/blob/master/GMXMMPBSA/createinput.py#L49-L310)

# Output Files Guide



Every gmx_MMPBSA calculation produces a structured set of output files that capture everything from raw energy vectors to final statistical summaries. Understanding these files is essential for interpreting your binding free energy results, diagnosing calculation issues, and feeding data into downstream analysis tools. This guide walks through each output file, explains its internal structure, and shows you how to locate the numbers that matter.

## Output File Landscape

The output system is orchestrated by two primary functions in [output_file.py](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py): `write_outputs` for the main results file and `write_decomp_output` for decomposition analysis. Both functions are invoked at the end of the calculation pipeline in [app.py](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L109-L110) after `parse_output_files()` has collected and organized the per-frame energy data. The following diagram shows how raw computation results flow into the files you will actually read.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Computation["Energy Calculation Phase"]
        GB["GB/PB/RISM<br/>Per-frame energies"]
        NMODE["NMODE<br/>Entropy data"]
        IE["Interaction Entropy"]
        C2["C2 Entropy"]
        QH["Quasi-Harmonic"]
    end

    subgraph Parsing["Output Parsing Phase"]
        AO["AmberOutput classes<br/>(amber_outputs.py)"]
        BS["BindingStatistics"]
        DO["DecompOut / DecompBinding"]
    end

    subgraph FinalOutput["Final Output Files"]
        FR["FINAL_RESULTS_<br/>MMPBSA.dat"]
        FD["FINAL_DECOMP_<br/>MMPBSA.dat"]
        CSV["Energy CSV files"]
        INFO["_MMPBSA_info"]
    end

    GB --> AO
    NMODE --> AO
    IE --> AO
    C2 --> AO
    QH --> AO
    AO --> BS
    AO --> DO
    BS --> FR
    DO --> FD
    BS --> CSV
    AO --> INFO
```

Sources: [output_file.py](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L53-L54), [output_file.py](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L395-L396), [app.py](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L109-L110)

## The Main Results File

The primary output of any gmx_MMPBSA run is the final results file, named **`FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA.dat`** by default (configurable via the `output` input variable). This file is written by the `write_outputs` function in [output_file.py](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L53) using the `OutputFile` class defined at [line 494](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L494). It contains a complete record of your calculation: input parameters, entropy results, per-component energy tables, and the final binding free energy values.

### File Header

The file opens with metadata that uniquely identifies the calculation session. The `OutputFile.write_date()` method [writes a timestamp](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L533-L536), followed by `print_file_info()` which [lists every input file](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L540-L606) — the GROMACS TPR structure, topology files, AMBER prmtop files, and initial trajectory paths. For binding calculations (not stability), the receptor and ligand masks are also printed along with the ligand residue name when the ligand is a single residue.

Below the file listing, a block of descriptive comments records the calculation parameters:

- **Number of frames** used for each calculation type
- **Solvent model** (GB surface area method: LCPO or molsurf)
- **PB solver** type (internal PBSA or iAPBS interface)
- **Temperature** in Kelvin
- **Units** declaration (all values in kcal/mol)
- **Statistics methodology** note explaining SD vs SD(Prop.)

Sources: [output_file.py](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L67-L117), [output_file.py](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L540-L606)

### Entropy Results Section

If any entropy approximation was requested, those results appear first in the output file. The `write_outputs` function processes entropy results [before free energy results](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L119-L267) in this order:

1. **Quasi-Harmonic (QH) entropy** — printed via `QHout.summary_output()` [at line 129](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L129)
2. **Interaction Entropy (IE)** — printed per-method (GB, PB, RISM, GBNSR6) [at lines 154-193](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L154-L193)
3. **C2 Entropy** — printed per-method [at lines 195-228](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L195-L228)
4. **Normal Mode (NMODE) entropy** — printed [at lines 231-265](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L231-L265)

Each entropy section reports the model used, the interaction energy standard deviation σ, the entropy value itself, its standard deviation, and the 95% confidence interval. For C2 entropy, the confidence interval is obtained through bootstrapping with 2000 re-samplings.

> [!TIP]
> **Critical reliability check**: If the interaction energy standard deviation σ exceeds 3.6 kcal/mol (~15 kJ/mol), gmx_MMPBSA automatically prints a **WARNING** [at line 190](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L190-L193) indicating that the IE or C2 entropy values are not reliable. This threshold is based on published recommendations. Always verify this before citing entropy-corrected binding free energies.

### Free Energy Results Section

After entropy data, the main energy tables appear. The `write_outputs` function [iterates through solvation models](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L268-L273) in order: GB, PB, 3D-RISM (standard, Gaussian fluctuation, PC+), and GBNSR6. Each model's results are written in a structured block with a section header like `GENERALIZED BORN:` or `POISSON BOLTZMANN:`.

For **binding** calculations, each solvation model produces four energy tables:

| Table | Description | Corresponding Code |
|-------|-------------|--------------------|
| **Complex** | Energy components for the full complex | `app.calc_types.normal[key]['complex'].summary_output()` [L286](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L286) |
| **Receptor** | Energy components for the isolated receptor | `app.calc_types.normal[key]['receptor'].summary_output()` [L287](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L287) |
| **Ligand** | Energy components for the isolated ligand | `app.calc_types.normal[key]['ligand'].summary_output()` [L288](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L288) |
| **Delta (Complex − Receptor − Ligand)** | Binding energy decomposition | `sys_norm.summary_output()` [L289](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L289) |

For **stability** calculations, only the Complex table is printed.

### Understanding the Energy Components

Each energy table contains rows for individual energy terms, composite sums, and five statistical columns. Here is what each term represents:

| Energy Term | Full Name | Description |
|------------|-----------|-------------|
| **BOND** | Bond stretching | Harmonic bond potential energy |
| **ANGLE** | Angle bending | Harmonic angle potential energy |
| **DIHED** | Dihedral torsion | Torsional and improper dihedral energy |
| **VDWAALS** | van der Waals | Lennard-Jones 6-12 potential |
| **EEL** | Electrostatic | Coulombic electrostatic energy |
| **1-4 VDW** | 1-4 van der Waals | Non-bonded VDW for atoms separated by 3 bonds |
| **1-4 EEL** | 1-4 Electrostatic | Non-bonded electrostatics for 1-4 atom pairs |
| **EGB** / **EPB** | Polar solvation | Electrostatic contribution to solvation free energy |
| **ESURF** / **ENPOLAR + EDISPER** | Non-polar solvation | Surface area and dispersion terms |
| **GGAS** | Gas-phase energy | = BOND + ANGLE + DIHED + VDWAALS + EEL + 1-4 VDW + 1-4 EEL |
| **GSOLV** | Solvation free energy | = EGB (or EPB) + ESURF |
| **TOTAL** | Total free energy | = GGAS + GSOLV |

### Statistics Columns

Each energy term is reported with five statistical measures. These are computed in the `BindingStatistics` class within [amber_outputs.py](GMXMMPBSA/amber_outputs.py#L956-L1135):

| Column | Meaning | Method |
|--------|---------|--------|
| **Average** | Mean energy across all frames | Simple arithmetic mean |
| **SD** | Sample standard deviation | Computed from the frame-by-frame array of values |
| **SEM** | Standard error of the mean | SD / √N from the frame array |
| **SD(Prop.)** | Propagated standard deviation | Error propagation formula for f = A − B − C |
| **SEM(Prop.)** | Propagated standard error | SD(Prop.) / √N |

For the delta (binding) energies, two standard deviations are reported because the delta is a derived quantity (Complex − Receptor − Ligand). The **SD** and **SEM** columns are computed from the array of per-frame delta values. The **SD(Prop.)** and **SEM(Prop.)** columns use the propagation of uncertainty formula, which treats each term's variance independently. When a single-trajectory protocol is used, bond, angle, dihedral, and 1-4 terms should be identically zero in the delta — if they are not, an inconsistency warning is printed [via `report_inconsistency()`](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L284-L285).

### Final Binding Free Energy

At the bottom of each solvation model section, if an entropy approximation was enabled, gmx_MMPBSA combines the TOTAL energy with the entropy correction to produce the final binding free energy:

**ΔG binding = ΔTOTAL − TΔS**

This is printed for each applicable entropy method (NMODE, IE, C2, QH) [at lines 297-316](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L297-L316). For example, when C2 entropy is used with GB, the output will show:

```
Using C2 Entropy Approximation:
ΔG binding =  -48.07 +/-  2.20
```

The uncertainty combines the variance from the TOTAL energy and the entropy term using the `utils.calc_sum` helper function.

Sources: [output_file.py](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L268-L316), [amber_outputs.py](GMXMMPBSA/amber_outputs.py#L956-L1135)

### Alanine Scanning Results

When alanine scanning is enabled (via the `ala` namelist), the output file includes additional sections for the **mutant** system and the **ΔΔ** comparison. The structure mirrors the normal results:

1. **Mutant energy tables** — Complex, Receptor, Ligand, and Delta for the mutated system [L318-L334](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L318-L334)
2. **ΔΔH binding** — the difference between mutant and wild-type binding enthalpies [L360-L361](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L360-L361)
3. **ΔΔG binding** — if entropy was calculated, ΔΔG is also reported for each entropy method [L363-L386](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L363-L386)

> [!TIP]
> **Alanine scanning output structure**: The mutant-specific output blocks appear immediately after each solvation model's normal results. If `mutant_only` is set (via `mutant_only=1` in the input file), the normal system results are skipped entirely and only mutant data is printed.

## The Decomposition Output File

When decomposition analysis is enabled (`decomprun=1`), a separate file named **`FINAL_DECOMP_MMPBSA.dat`** is created. This file is written by the `write_decomp_output` function [at line 395](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L395-L491) and can be produced in either **ASCII** or **CSV** format (controlled by `csv_format` in the `decomp` namelist, defaulting to CSV since v1.5.0).

### Decomposition Table Structure

For each solvation model (GB, PB, or GBNSR6), the decomposition output contains per-residue energy breakdowns across three subsystems (Complex, Receptor, Ligand) and three decomposition types, plus the delta values:

| Section | Decomposition Type | Description |
|---------|-------------------|-------------|
| **Total Energy Decomposition** | TDC | Full residue energy = Sidechain + Backbone |
| **Sidechain Energy Decomposition** | SDC | Only sidechain atom contributions |
| **Backbone Energy Decomposition** | BDC | Only backbone atom contributions |
| **Delta Energies** | Δ | Complex − Receptor − Ligand for each decomposition type |

Each residue row reports six energy columns — **Internal** (bonded terms), **van der Waals**, **Electrostatic**, **Polar Solvation**, **Non-Polar Solvation**, and **TOTAL** — each with Average, Std. Dev., and Std. Err. of Mean. The delta section additionally includes a **Location** column (R for receptor residue, L for ligand residue) to identify the origin of each residue.

### Decomposition Output Modes

The `csv_format` parameter in the `decomp` namelist [controls the output format](GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L647):

- **`csv_format=1`** (default): Writes a CSV file with comma-separated values, easily importable into spreadsheet software or plotting tools
- **`csv_format=0`**: Writes a human-readable ASCII table format with aligned columns

Sources: [output_file.py](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L410-L443), [input_parser.py](GMXMMPBSA/input_parser.py#L642-L648)

## Energy Vector CSV Files

In addition to the formatted output files, gmx_MMPBSA can produce **CSV files containing per-frame energy vectors**. These are raw data files where each row corresponds to one snapshot and each column is an energy term. This is particularly useful for custom analysis, plotting in external tools, or statistical testing.

There are two energy vector output files:

| File | Controlled By | Contains |
|------|--------------|----------|
| Main energy CSV | `force_norest` / default naming | Per-frame energies for Complex, Receptor, Ligand, and Delta |
| Decomposition energy CSV | `dec_energies` naming | Per-frame per-residue decomposition energies |

These files are generated when `FILES.energyout` or `FILES.dec_energies` are set, and the data is dumped via `_print_vectors()` methods on the respective output classes [L291-L294](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L291-L294). The `BindingStatistics._print_vectors()` method [at line 1016](GMXMMPBSA/amber_outputs.py#L1016-L1047) handles the main energy CSV output.

Sources: [output_file.py](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L88-L92), [amber_outputs.py](GMXMMPBSA/amber_outputs.py#L1016-L1047)

## The Info File (_MMPBSA_info)

The `_MMPBSA_info` file is a serialized backup of the entire calculation state, created by the `InfoFile` class in [infofile.py](GMXMMPBSA/infofile.py#L63-L139). Its purpose is to enable **post-processing** — re-running the output generation or analysis without re-executing the full energy calculation. The `write_info` method [at line 86](GMXMMPBSA/infofile.py#L86-L137) saves all input variables, file paths, frame counts, and calculation configuration. The `read_info` method [at line 139](GMXMMPBSA/infofile.py#L139-L218) restores this state into the `MMPBSA_App` object.

When you use the `--rewrite-output` flag, gmx_MMPBSA skips the entire calculation phase and instead loads the info file to regenerate the final output files [L103-L106](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L103-L106):

```python
info = InfoFile(app, True)
info.read_info()
app.loadcheck_prmtops()
# Then proceeds to parse_output_files() and write_final_outputs()
```

This is useful when you want to change output formatting or verbosity without spending hours recomputing energies.

Sources: [infofile.py](GMXMMPBSA/infofile.py#L63-L139), [app.py](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L103-L106)

## The Compact Results File

gmx_MMPBSA also generates a **`COMPACT_MMXSA_RESULTS.mmxsa`** file via the `data2pkl` function [at line 31](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L31-L51). This is a Python pickle file that bundles the input parameters, file information, calculation types, and the full text content of the output files into a single binary object. It is designed for use with the **gmx_MMPBSA analyzer** GUI tool, which reads this file to enable interactive visualization without requiring access to the original calculation data.

Sources: [output_file.py](GMXMMPBSA/output_file.py#L31-L51)

## Log File

The **`gmx_MMPBSA.log`** file captures all logging output from the calculation. It is initialized at the start of the `gmxmmpbsa()` function [at line 49](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L49) with both DEBUG-level file logging and INFO-level console output. This file is your primary resource for diagnosing calculation failures, understanding which steps completed successfully, and tracing any warnings or errors that occurred during topology conversion, trajectory processing, or energy computation.

Sources: [app.py](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L41-L50)

## Complete Output File Summary

The table below consolidates every output file you may encounter, its default naming, format, and content:

| File | Default Name | Format | Content |
|------|-------------|--------|---------|
| Main results | `FINAL_RESULTS_MMPBSA.dat` | ASCII text | Header, entropy results, energy tables, binding free energies |
| Decomposition results | `FINAL_DECOMP_MMPBSA.dat` | ASCII or CSV | Per-residue decomposition energies by subsystem |
| Main energy vectors | (configurable) | CSV | Per-frame energy values for all terms |
| Decomp energy vectors | (configurable) | CSV | Per-frame per-residue decomposition values |
| Info file | `_MMPBSA_info` | Serialized | Full calculation state for post-processing |
| Compact results | `COMPACT_MMXSA_RESULTS.mmxsa` | Python pickle | Bundled data for the analyzer GUI |
| Log file | `gmx_MMPBSA.log` | Text | All runtime logging messages |

## Reading Your Results: A Quick Checklist

After a successful calculation, follow these steps to interpret your output:

1. **Check the header** — verify the input files, masks, and number of frames are correct
2. **Look for warnings** — scan for "WARNING" lines, especially about interaction energy σ > 3.6 kcal/mol or inconsistency flags
3. **Review entropy values** — confirm they are physically reasonable (typically −TΔS between −5 and −30 kcal/mol for protein-ligand systems)
4. **Examine the delta energy table** — the ΔVDWAALS and ΔEEL rows reveal the driving forces behind binding
5. **Read the final ΔG binding** — this is the bottom-line result that combines ΔTOTAL with entropy
6. **For decomposition** — open the CSV in a spreadsheet to identify hotspot residues with large favorable or unfavorable contributions

For interactive visualization of these results, see the [Interactive Visualization](16-interactive-visualization) guide. To understand how these energies were computed from your GROMACS trajectories, continue to the [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview). For detailed parameter control over output formatting, refer to the [Input File Reference](3-input-file-reference).

# Architecture Overview



gmx_MMPBSA is an end-state free energy calculation tool that bridges the GROMACS molecular dynamics ecosystem with AMBER's MM/PBSA methodology. Its architecture follows a **sequential pipeline pattern** where user-supplied GROMACS coordinates and topologies are converted into AMBER-compatible formats, processed through solvation energy calculations, and distilled into statistical free energy estimates. Understanding this pipeline is essential for anyone looking to extend the tool, debug calculation failures, or integrate its results into custom analysis workflows.

## High-Level Pipeline

The entire system can be understood as a directed pipeline with three distinct phases — **preparation**, **computation**, and **analysis** — each encapsulated by dedicated module clusters. The entry points funnel through a single application class, ensuring all configuration, validation, and orchestration logic remains centralized.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph EntryPoints["Entry Points (app.py)"]
        CLI["gmx_MMPBSA<br/>CLI invocation"]
        ANA["gmx_MMPBSA_ana<br/>GUI Analyzer"]
        TST["gmx_MMPBSA_test<br/>Test Suite"]
    end

    subgraph Preparation["Phase 1 — Preparation"]
        CLP["commandlineparser.py<br/>CLI argument parsing"]
        INP["input_parser.py<br/>Input file parsing"]
        MKTOP["make_top.py<br/>GROMACS → Amber topology"]
        MKTRAJ["make_trajs.py<br/>Trajectory stripping & formatting"]
        PARM["parm_setup.py<br/>System mapping & mask resolution"]
        CINP["createinput.py<br/>Sander input file generation"]
    end

    subgraph Computation["Phase 2 — Computation"]
        APP["MMPBSA_App (main.py)<br/>Orchestrator"]
        CALC["calculation.py<br/>Calculation class hierarchy"]
        EXT["External Engines<br/>mmpbsa_py_energy · sander · cpptraj"]
    end

    subgraph Analysis["Phase 3 — Analysis"]
        AMB["amber_outputs.py<br/>Output parsing & statistics"]
        OUT["output_file.py<br/>Final report generation"]
        INFO["infofile.py<br/>State serialization"]
        API["API.py<br/>Programmatic data access"]
        GUI["analyzer/<br/>Interactive visualization"]
    end

    CLI --> CLP
    CLI --> INP
    CLP --> APP
    INP --> APP
    APP --> MKTOP
    APP --> MKTRAJ
    MKTOP --> PARM
    APP --> CINP
    CINP --> CALC
    MKTRAJ --> CALC
    PARM --> CALC
    CALC --> EXT
    EXT --> AMB
    AMB --> OUT
    AMB --> INFO
    INFO --> API
    INFO --> ANA
    APP --> OUT

    style APP fill:#2d6a4f,color:#fff,stroke:#1b4332
    style CALC fill:#40916c,color:#fff
    style API fill:#40916c,color:#fff
```

This diagram reveals the most important architectural truth about gmx_MMPBSA: the `MMPBSA_App` class in [main.py](GMXMMPBSA/main.py#L64-L76) is the **single orchestrator** that owns the entire calculation lifecycle. Every other module is a worker invoked by or through this class.

## Module Inventory and Responsibilities

The codebase comprises approximately 20 Python modules within the `GMXMMPBSA/` package, each with a clearly delineated responsibility. The following table maps each module to its architectural role and approximate complexity:

| Module | Role | Key Class/Function | Lines |
|---|---|---|---|
| [main.py](GMXMMPBSA/main.py#L64-L76) | **Central orchestrator** | `MMPBSA_App` | ~1526 |
| [app.py](GMXMMPBSA/app.py#L40-L114) | **Entry point router** | `gmxmmpbsa()`, `gmxmmpbsa_ana()` | 167 |
